hook_text: A factory's books look perfect while a village boils its water. Economics explains the trick in one sentence.
clip_script: A brick kiln operates upstream of a village. Its waste pipe empties into the river and pays nothing for the privilege. Downstream, mothers boil drinking water, the fish traps come up empty, and the clinic's queue lengthens every month. Open the kiln's account books and the business looks superb — because its largest production cost is being settled by families who appear nowhere in those books. Economists call that hidden invoice an externality. Why is the river treated in a way no one would treat their own vegetable garden? Because the garden has an owner and the river does not. Whatever everybody owns, nobody protects — watch two fishermen race a shared pool to the last fin, because any fish spared tonight sits in the other man's trap by morning. So here is the diagnosis in one line: the market damages the environment not because people are wicked, but because the damage is priced at zero. And every fix you will ever study is one repair, attempted four ways — put the missing price back: a rule, a tax, a reward, or an owner.
visual_style: A split river scene: a kiln's ledger glowing green upstream while red cost tags — firewood, clinic, empty traps — pile up over a village downstream; two rowboats racing for one last fish; a giant R0 price tag on the river that flips, at the end, into four tags labelled RULE, TAX, REWARD, OWNER.
pacing: Slow reveal of the hidden invoice, a beat on the racing boats, crisp snap onto the priced-at-zero line and the four tags.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn how a price tag can guard a river — and a planet.
